description: Exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism, ecumenism and inter-faith dialogue; national identity and proselytisation.
content_html:
How Do Religions See Each Other?

One of the most significant questions facing religious communities in the twenty-first century is: what do we make of people who hold different beliefs? Historically, many religious traditions taught that they alone possessed the full truth. Today, living in a diverse and interconnected world, that position is frequently contested both within and between religious communities. Theologians have developed three broad models to describe different religious attitudes to one another: exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism.

Exclusivism holds that one religion is the sole path to salvation and that other religions, however sincere, cannot offer what their followers need. This position draws on strong scriptural traditions. In Christianity, John 14:6 records Jesus saying: “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Taken in an exclusivist direction, this means non-Christians cannot reach God through their own traditions. In Islam, the concept of Islam as the final and complete revelation builds a similar logic, though Islamic theology also affirms the validity of earlier prophets. The exclusivist position is internally consistent and takes its own scriptures seriously, but critics argue it is arrogant and incompatible with a diverse society.

Inclusivism is a mediating position. It maintains that one’s own religion is the fullest or most complete truth, but recognises that God can work through other traditions. The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) moved the Catholic Church significantly towards inclusivism by affirming that non-Christian religions “often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all men.” This means Catholics can affirm the goodness in other traditions while still believing that the fullness of revelation is found in Christ. Many moderate believers across traditions hold inclusivist positions.

Pluralism goes further: it holds that all major world religions are genuinely valid and equally effective paths to ultimate reality. The philosopher and theologian John Hick argued that what different religions call “God” or “ultimate reality” is the same reality, encountered differently through different cultural lenses. Hick described the relationship between religions using the image of different paths up the same mountain. Pluralism is attractive as a foundation for inter-faith dialogue but is criticised by exclusivists and some inclusivists as relativistic — implying that doctrinal differences do not ultimately matter.

Ecumenism: Dialogue Within Christianity

Ecumenism refers specifically to dialogue and cooperation within Christianity — between denominations such as the Church of England, the Catholic Church, the Methodist Church, and the Orthodox churches. The word comes from the Greek oikoumene, meaning “the whole inhabited world.” Ecumenism recognises that, despite significant differences in doctrine, practice and church authority, Christian churches share core beliefs in the Trinity, the authority of scripture, and the lordship of Jesus Christ.

This intra-faith communication has produced visible results. The World Council of Churches (WCC), founded in 1948 and based in Geneva, brings together over 350 member churches from Protestant, Orthodox, Anglican and other traditions. It campaigns on issues of global justice, peace and human rights, and holds regular assemblies where churches seek consensus on shared challenges. The Churches Together movement in Britain coordinates local and national ecumenical activity, enabling churches from different denominations to worship, serve and campaign together.

Key Fact

The World Council of Churches (founded 1948, Geneva) unites over 350 member churches from Protestant, Orthodox and Anglican traditions. The Churches Together movement in Britain coordinates local and national ecumenical activity. Both demonstrate that Christian unity is sought through cooperation even where full doctrinal agreement has not been reached.

Inter-Faith Dialogue in Modern Britain

Inter-faith dialogue extends across religious boundaries: between Christianity and Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism and other faiths. In twenty-first century Britain — one of the most religiously diverse societies in the world — inter-faith dialogue is increasingly necessary. It operates at local level (inter-faith groups, shared community projects) and national level (the Inter Faith Network for the UK, the Faith and Belief Forum).

Christians who support inter-faith dialogue often point to Matthew 22:37–40, where Jesus identifies love of God and love of neighbour as the greatest commandments. If neighbours include people of other faiths, then relationship and understanding become a religious duty. Jewish teaching on human dignity (every person made b'tselem Elohim — in the image of God) similarly points toward respect for all. Muslims who engage in dialogue often refer to the Qur’anic principle that God could have made all people one community but chose diversity so that people “may come to know one another.”

Proselytisation — seeking to convert others — creates tension with inter-faith dialogue. If the goal of engagement is ultimately to win converts, then dialogue becomes a form of sales rather than genuine mutual understanding. Matthew 28:18–20 records the “Great Commission”: Jesus commanding his disciples to “go and make disciples of all nations.” John 14:2 speaks of “many rooms” in the Father’s house — which some read as inclusive, others as suggesting that belonging to Christ is necessary to receive them.

Many Christians today distinguish between witnessing (living and speaking in a way that reflects their faith, leaving others free to respond) and proselytising (using pressure or inducement to secure conversion). Inter-faith practitioners generally agree that genuine dialogue requires each party to bring their own convictions honestly, without any hidden agenda of conversion. This means the Great Commission and inter-faith dialogue are not necessarily incompatible — but they must be held in tension carefully.

Religion and National Identity

The relationship between religion and national identity is complex. In England, being Christian has historically been part of what it means to be English or British — the head of state is Christian, Christian values are embedded in law and custom, and Christian symbols appear on national flags and currency. As Britain has become more religiously diverse, this identification has become contested.

For some Christians, the identification of Christianity with British identity is a resource: it provides a moral framework for national life and a basis for shared values. For religious minorities — British Muslims, Sikhs, Hindus, Jews, Buddhists — the equation of national with Christian identity can feel excluding, as though full belonging requires religious conformity. Secular commentators argue that national identity should be grounded in civic values (democracy, rule of law, freedom of speech) rather than in any particular religious tradition. The debate is not simply between religion and secularism but within religious communities themselves: many British Christians are strong advocates for multiculturalism and religious equality, seeing these as expressions of their faith.

Key Fact

John 14:6 (“I am the way, the truth and the life”) is used by exclusivists to argue that salvation requires faith in Christ. Matthew 22:37–40 (love God and love your neighbour) is used by inclusivists and pluralists to ground inter-faith dialogue. Matthew 28:18–20 (the Great Commission) raises the question of whether evangelism and dialogue can coexist.

Key Concepts: Diversity, Freedom and Consensus

The key philosophical concepts in this lesson — consensus, diversity, uniformity, freedom of choice, and freedom of expression — are not religious or secular in themselves. They describe the conditions under which any meaningful dialogue can take place. Genuine consensus respects difference rather than demanding uniformity. Freedom of choice means individuals may convert, leave a religion, or hold no religion at all. Freedom of expression allows religious believers to articulate their convictions in public debate, and allows critics of religion to challenge those convictions. These values are most tested when religious communities hold positions that others find deeply disagreeable — which is precisely when commitment to them matters most.
exam_tip_html: This lesson has a high AO2 load — you must analyse and evaluate rather than simply describe. For “Explain” questions (6 marks), define the key term precisely first: for example, exclusivism is not the same as intolerance; it is a theological claim about the uniqueness of salvation. For the 15-mark “Discuss”, avoid treating “all exclusivists are intolerant” as a given — this is a weak analysis. A strong response will show that sincere religious conviction can be exclusivist and still respectful. Common misspellings include ‘ecumenicism’ (correct: ‘ecumenism’) and ‘proselytization’ — use ‘proselytisation’. Spelling of ‘exclusivism’ and ‘pluralism’ is rewarded in SPaG marks on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three models describe how religions relate to one another: exclusivism (only one religion leads to salvation — anchored in John 14:6), inclusivism (one religion is fullest but others contain truth), and pluralism (all major religions are equally valid paths to the same reality).
  • Ecumenism is dialogue within Christianity; the World Council of Churches and Churches Together are key examples. Intra-faith communication reduces division within the same tradition.
  • Inter-faith dialogue across religious boundaries is increasingly important in diverse societies. Matthew 22:37–40 (“love your neighbour”) underpins many Christians’ commitment to it. Proselytisation creates tension with dialogue: the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) must be distinguished from unethical pressure to convert.
  • Religion and national identity are intertwined in Britain but increasingly contested. The key philosophical values — diversity, freedom of choice, freedom of expression, and genuine consensus — provide the conditions for sustainable dialogue.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'exclusivism' in the context of religious dialogue.
practice_questions.marks: The belief that one's own religion is the only true path to salvation/ultimate truth (and that other religions cannot offer salvation/are false). [1 mark]

Credit responses that include: the movement seeking greater cooperation/understanding/unity among different Christian denominations (1 mark); reference to dialogue, shared worship or joint campaigns across denominations, e.g. Churches Together / World Council of Churches (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any of: exclusivism holds only one religion leads to salvation; inclusivism holds one religion is fullest/truest but others contain elements of truth; pluralism holds all major religions are equally valid paths. A fourth point could contrast the evangelical implications: exclusivism implies the importance of conversion; pluralism implies conversion is unnecessary. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why inter-faith dialogue is important in modern Britain.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Responses may include:
• Britain is one of the most religiously diverse societies in the world; dialogue reduces misunderstanding and prejudice between communities. Matthew 22:37–40 (love your neighbour) grounds this for Christians as a religious duty, not just a civic one.
• After events such as the 7/7 bombings or the Christchurch attacks, inter-faith dialogue is a tool for building resilience against extremism by creating relationships of trust between communities.
• John Hick's pluralist argument suggests that different religions encounter the same ultimate reality; dialogue can deepen each community's understanding of that reality.
• Many Christians believe the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) requires honest dialogue as a form of witness, which can be done respectfully alongside genuine listening.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 for identifying the reason, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Proselytisation and genuine inter-faith dialogue cannot coexist.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• If the aim of dialogue is ultimately to convert the other person, then it is not genuine dialogue but a form of persuasion. The other participant’s views are not taken seriously on their own terms.
• Religious minorities in Britain have historically experienced pressure to convert (e.g. colonial mission contexts); this history makes trust difficult when majority groups pursue outreach alongside dialogue.
• Pluralists such as John Hick argue that if all paths lead to the same reality, seeking to convert others is unnecessary and potentially arrogant.

Arguments against:
• Many Christians distinguish between witnessing (living out faith openly) and proselytising (using pressure or inducement). The Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) calls Christians to share the gospel — this can be done respectfully alongside genuine listening.
• Freedom of expression includes the freedom to share one’s beliefs and invite others to consider them. A society that bans persuasion restricts religious freedom.
• Exclusivist Christians, Muslims and others sincerely believe they possess truth that is important for others; concealing this belief in the name of dialogue would itself be dishonest.
• Many inter-faith practitioners say honest dialogue requires each party to bring their real convictions — including the belief that their tradition is true — provided they do not use manipulation or pressure.

Mastering (13–15 marks): Both sides fully developed with specific examples (Matthew 28:18–20, John Hick, freedom of expression); explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion on whether the two can coexist.
Secure (9–12 marks): Both sides explained with some development; at least one specific reference; conclusion reached.
Developing (5–8 marks): One side more developed; limited specific references; partial conclusion.
Emerging (1–4 marks): Brief, one-sided or largely descriptive. [15 marks including SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'pluralism' as a religious attitude.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the view that all major world religions are equally valid (1 mark); paths to the same ultimate reality / salvation (1 mark). Reference to John Hick's analogy of different paths up the same mountain may be credited. [2 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which theological position holds that all major world religions are equally valid paths to the same ultimate reality?
Which verse is most commonly used by Christian exclusivists to argue that salvation requires faith in Christ?
The movement seeking greater cooperation and unity among different Christian denominations is called _____.
The World Council of Churches was founded in _____ and is based in Geneva.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Only one religion leads to salvation; others cannot offer the same truth
One's own religion is fullest, but elements of truth may exist in others
The active attempt to persuade others to convert to one's own religion

flashcard_questions.a: The belief that one's own religion is the only true path to salvation and that other religions are false.
The belief that one's own religion offers the fullest truth but that elements of truth may exist in other religions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is pluralism in the context of religious dialogue?
flashcard_questions.a: The view that all major world religions are equally valid paths to the same ultimate reality.

flashcard_questions.q: Which philosopher and theologian argued that different religions are like different paths up the same mountain?

flashcard_questions.a: The movement working to build unity and cooperation among different Christian denominations.
Dialogue and cooperation among different congregations or denominations within a single religious tradition.

flashcard_questions.q: What body was founded in 1948 and unites over 350 Christian churches from different traditions?
flashcard_questions.a: The World Council of Churches, based in Geneva.
Structured conversation and cooperation between people of different religious traditions, aimed at mutual understanding.

flashcard_questions.q: Which verse records Jesus giving the 'Great Commission' to make disciples of all nations?

flashcard_questions.a: The active attempt to persuade others to convert to one's own religion.

flashcard_questions.q: What commandment in Matthew 22:37–40 grounds inter-faith dialogue for many Christians?
flashcard_questions.a: Love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinction do many Christians make between witnessing and proselytising?
flashcard_questions.a: Witnessing means living and speaking openly about faith; proselytising involves pressure or inducement to convert.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that one's own religion is the only true path to salvation or ultimate truth, and that other religions are false.
The belief that while one's own religion offers the fullest truth, elements of truth and salvation may be found in other religions.
The view that all major world religions are equally valid paths to the same ultimate reality or salvation.
The movement seeking greater cooperation, understanding and unity among different Christian denominations.
Dialogue and cooperation among different congregations or denominations within a single religious tradition.
Structured conversation and cooperation between people of different religious traditions, aimed at mutual understanding and reducing prejudice.
The active attempt to persuade others to convert to one's own religion.
A shared sense of belonging to a nation, which in Britain has historically been intertwined with Christian heritage and symbols.
